description: We are (two) three students from Europe who like space.
summary:
Landing near the Moon's south pole is a puzzle of light and radio. The Sun barely climbs above the horizon, mountains cast shadows that stretch for kilometres, and a spot that is bright one day can be dark the next. Earth, which a lander needs to talk to, can be hidden behind a ridge just as easily. Planners have to compare sites and dates quickly, but the tools that hold this data are built for specialists.

LunaScout is our attempt to make that comparison simple. You open an interactive 3D Moon, pick a landing site (from NASA's candidate list or anywhere you click), and press play on a timeline. The Sun and Earth move around the Moon where NASA's JPL ephemeris puts them, and the app shows what each part of the site really sees: how much sunlight reaches it, whether Earth is in view, how long the longest day and longest darkness last, and how much power a solar panel would get. It's all calculated on real NASA laser-altimeter terrain, so mountains and craters really do cast shadows.

Put two sites side by side and you see in seconds how a change of place or launch date changes the picture. It's built for mission planners, but we wanted a student or a curious member of the public to understand it too.
details:
The idea: Choosing where and when to land near the Moon's south pole comes down to two questions: will the lander have power, and can it talk to Earth? Both depend on tiny differences in place and date. The Sun skims the horizon, so a ridge a few hundred metres away can put a site in shadow for days. Earth can disappear behind the same ridge. Planners have to answer these questions again every time a launch slips or a site changes, and the data lives in tools built for experts. We wanted one place where anyone can pick a site and a date range and see the answer.

The app opens on a 3D Moon. The Sun and Earth sit where NASA's JPL ephemeris says they are, and you can zoom from space down to the mountains and craters of a candidate site, with the terrain getting more detailed as you get closer. Press play on the timeline and the Sun and Earth move around the Moon. For each site you get sunlight, Earth visibility, power, and the key operational numbers: when the Sun and Earth rise and set, the longest day, the longest darkness, and how long Earth is in view. A switch changes to a flat map of the pole. You can also show the rays from the Sun and Earth, to see where terrain blocks them. The Compare mode puts two sites next to each other with one shared timeline and a scorecard that marks the better site for each measure. It also shows NASA's long-term averages for each place, so you can tell a bad day from a bad location.

How it works: We take real NASA laser-altimeter terrain and trace light rays across it, from the Sun and Earth to many points on the site. That's how mountains and craters cast real shadows, instead of a flat estimate. Sun and Earth positions come from JPL Horizons. We treat the Sun as a disk, not a point, so partial shadow shows up correctly. We built it for speed, so results appear while you explore.

For everyone: The same screens work for a planner who wants detail and for a student who just wants to see why the Moon is hard. We hide detail behind a "more" section, use plain language, and keep the Moon still while the sky moves, so the view doesn't cause motion sickness.

Our limits: Earth coverage is a line-of-sight calculation, not a signal-strength model. Much of the finest terrain is interpolated between laser tracks. We don't model reflected light, and the tool covers 60°S–90°S.

Tools: Python, FastAPI, NumPy, Numba and SPICE for the science; React, TypeScript, Three.js and OpenLayers for the interface. We built it with help from AI coding tools, described in the next section.
